Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

issues.item: Triggers: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: The trigger profile is dominated by interpersonal closeness plus taste and crying. For torture, gustatory and affective-expression triggers are plausible, but emotional closeness as a primary trigger is less well integrated with the rest of the profile, which contains no interpersonal betrayal/shame/relationship-based appraisals or memories to explain why closeness itself would be a salient cue. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a direct impossibility.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the formulation. The strongest active pathways involve triggers, negative appraisals, memory, and threat, but the other selected strategies are control/safety based (restrict eating, hypervigilance), whereas gambling is a sensation-seeking/distracting behavior with no support from the memory, threat, or appraisal items. It reads like a separate coping pattern rather than part of the same PTSD-maintaining loop.

'Concentration' is not a threat belief/state in the same way as the other threat items. 'Cannot Trust Safety' and 'Body Reacts Before Mind' reflect ongoing sense of current threat, but concentration difficulty is a nonspecific cognitive symptom and does not cohere tightly within the Threat node. Given the formulation emphasizes Memory → Threat and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a more direct threat-related item would be expected.

vignette:
Asha Malik is a 47-year-old South Asian woman who has lived most of her adult life in the United States and is now divorced, though she still carries herself with the measured composure of someone who has spent years in a public, caregiving role. She serves as a pastor in her community, a position that has long depended on her ability to sit with other people’s pain, speak calmly, and remain steady in moments of distress. That steadiness was shattered years ago when she was taken and held captive by a group of men who tortured her. When she tries to describe what happened, her account comes in broken fragments: one scene is painfully clear, while the next is simply gone. She remembers certain moments with a harsh precision—the feel of being restrained, the terror in a room she could not leave—but other parts of the ordeal remain blank, as if her mind has sealed them off. What returns most sharply are disconnected pieces that never fully join together, leaving her with the unsettling sense that she knows enough to be haunted but not enough to make sense of it.

Since then, Asha has been unable to trust safety when it is offered to her. She can be sitting in her church office, listening to a parishioner reassure her that she is secure, and still feel that the words do not reach her. She has come to believe that her body recognizes danger before her mind can catch up, and she describes this with a kind of weary certainty: her shoulders tense, her stomach tightens, and her heart starts racing before she has even had time to decide whether there is a real threat in the room. At church events, in crowded hallways, or while moving through parking lots after evening meetings, she finds herself scanning faces and entrances, superalert for dangerous people in a way that feels automatic and exhausting. Even when nothing is happening, she remains on guard, as though the next moment could turn without warning.

Certain reminders pull her abruptly back. She has identified a specific taste from the period of captivity that still unsettles her; if it appears in food, she can feel her chest tighten and her attention narrow around the memory of that time. Because of this, she has taken to controlling what she eats with unusual strictness, choosing and limiting foods with great care in an effort to feel some sense of control over her body and surroundings. At home she can spend long periods planning meals, avoiding anything that might carry that taste or even a faint resemblance to it. This has narrowed her daily routines and made eating feel less like nourishment than a guarded ritual.

Talking about what happened is especially difficult. When the topic comes up, even in a church context where she is expected to be compassionate and composed, she feels the urge to shut it down. She has tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing it away whenever it starts to surface, and she worries that if she allows herself to go there she will not be able to handle it. Crying is another potent trigger: when she sees someone cry, or when her own tears begin to rise unexpectedly, she is thrown into an immediate state of distress. The sight and sound of crying seem to open a door to the helplessness of the past, and she responds by tightening control over her expression, sometimes leaving a room early or turning to practical tasks so she does not have to stay with the feeling.

Asha’s sense of herself has been deeply shaken. She used to see pastoral care as something she could do naturally and reliably, but now she fears she is no longer capable of doing the things that once defined her. She has become preoccupied with the thought that simply thinking about the event will overwhelm her, and this has made it harder for her to remain present in the reflective, emotionally open work that her role requires. She can still perform many of the outward duties of ministry, but she experiences them as thinner and more effortful than before, as if she is trying to speak from behind a wall. In quieter moments, she has said with stark resignation that she has no future, a belief that sits beside her ongoing efforts to keep going. It was the accumulating burden of these experiences—the inability to trust safety, the strain of remaining watchful, the narrowing of her eating, the fear of discussing what happened, and the sense that her life had become smaller than the one she once knew—that eventually brought her to seek help. What she wants most is relief from the constant vigilance and the hope that she might one day feel safe in her own body again, even though part of her is afraid that the part of herself she lost to the torture may never return.
